all.title: Interactive System Development Life Cycle Stages

concepts.name: prototype
concepts.definition: A prototype is a lightweight implementation, with much lower requirements for resources, skilled manpower, and cost than a full implementation, that can be built quickly to model or demonstrate a design idea and to test whether it will work in practice. It can be discarded after testing or refined into the final product.

defining_facts.text: The design-prototype-evaluate cycle in experience design consists of designing, quickly prototyping the design, evaluating it, finding problems, refining the design, and repeating this with new prototypes and evaluations, which may require many cycles before the design is stabilized.

Quick evaluation of design ideas in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle requires both a prototype that models or demonstrates the design idea and can be built quickly, and a quick evaluation method for testing the prototype; both requirements are equally important for a quick execution of the cycle.
Prototyping techniques are used for quick prototyping and quick evaluation of a prototype, and they are typically used to collect feedback on the usability of design ideas.

A prototype is a lightweight implementation, with much lower requirements for resources, skilled manpower, and cost than a full implementation, that is used to test whether a design idea will work in practice, so one does not always need to fully implement the idea first.

A prototype can be discarded after it has served its purpose of testing design ideas, or, in the best case, it can be incrementally refined and tested as development progresses until it evolves into the fully implemented final product.

concepts.name: interactive system
concepts.definition: Interactive system is a system in which interaction takes place between the computer or system and the user, a lay person who is not necessarily a technology expert and who wants to use the system rather than understand how it works.

defining_facts.text: Interactive computing systems, or interactive systems, are systems in which interaction takes place between the computer or system and the user.
In interactive systems, the user is a lay person or layman user who is not necessarily a technology expert and who wants to use the system rather than understand how the system works.
Designers of interactive systems that are intended to be used by laypersons should not force users to learn the underlying technology or understand the relevant technical terms.

concepts.name: error prevention
concepts.definition: Error prevention is a system design rule in which the design helps users prevent errors by aiming to keep error rates low, because user errors cannot be completely eliminated.

defining_facts.text: The fifth rule in system design is to offer error prevention and simple error handling.

In system design, user errors cannot be completely eliminated, so a design should aim to keep error rates low; for example, close and start options for the same interface should not be placed side by side because a user may accidentally choose the wrong action.

Nielsen's 10 heuristics consist of: 1) visibility of system status, in which the status of the system should be visible to the user; 2) match between system and the real world, in which what the user does on the system should closely match the user's real-world experience; 3) user control and freedom, concerning whether the user is given freedom and what kind of controls are provided; 4) consistency and standards, in which elements and layout should be consistent across different screens and standards should be followed; 5) error prevention, in which the design should help the user prevent errors; 6) recognition rather than recall, in which the user should not have to remember what to do but should be able to recognize from elements what to do because recollection is more difficult than recognition; 7) flexibility and efficiency of use; 8) aesthetic and minimalist design, in which the design should have a minimum number of elements and should be aesthetically pleasing; 9) help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors; and 10) help and documentation, in which the system should provide help and documentation support.

concepts.name: horizontal prototype
concepts.definition: Horizontal prototype is a prototype that depicts the entire interface at a surface level, showing its look, feel, and appearance without functionality or interaction, so it is used to discuss, brainstorm, and elicit feedback about whether the interface is understandable, intuitive, and usable.

defining_facts.text: Prototypes can be broadly considered in two categories, horizontal prototypes and vertical prototypes.

A horizontal prototype is a prototype that depicts the entire interface at a surface level, showing how the interface appears to the user in terms of look, feel, and appearance, without any functionality or interaction, so no real work can be done with it.

Horizontal prototypes are suitable for discussing, brainstorming, and eliciting user feedback about the look, feel, and appearance of an interface, including whether its appearance is understandable, intuitive, and usable.

In medium-fidelity prototyping, a computer used only to create static interface sketches produces a horizontal prototype because no real functionality is present, while an Adobe Flash animation video or a Microsoft PowerPoint (PPT) slideshow with simple key presses or timers can simulate interaction and create a vertical prototype.

Low-fidelity prototypes are primarily meant for horizontal prototypes, medium-fidelity approaches are primarily meant for both horizontal and vertical prototypes, and high-fidelity approaches are primarily meant for vertical prototypes, so making horizontal prototypes using a high-fidelity approach may not make much sense.

concepts.name: vertical prototype
concepts.definition: A vertical prototype is a type of prototype that implements a few selected features likely to be most commonly used in depth, from the first screen to the last, to represent interactions rather than all system functionalities.

defining_facts.text: Prototypes can be broadly considered in two categories, horizontal prototypes and vertical prototypes.

A vertical prototype primarily represents interactions or functionalities by implementing a few selected features likely to be most commonly used in practice, in depth from the first screen to the last screen after the last action is performed, not all functionalities, because that would amount to having the full system.
Vertical prototypes are suitable for analysis of interactions and features because they implement interactions.

In the description of a vertical prototype, the term implemented and the term screen are generic, so implemented does not necessarily mean writing code, and screen can refer to a two-dimensional (2D) computer screen or a scene in a virtual or immersive environment.

In medium-fidelity prototyping, a computer used only to create static interface sketches produces a horizontal prototype because no real functionality is present, while an Adobe Flash animation video or a Microsoft PowerPoint (PPT) slideshow with simple key presses or timers can simulate interaction and create a vertical prototype.

Low-fidelity prototypes are primarily meant for horizontal prototypes, medium-fidelity approaches are primarily meant for both horizontal and vertical prototypes, and high-fidelity approaches are primarily meant for vertical prototypes, so making horizontal prototypes using a high-fidelity approach may not make much sense.

concepts.name: low-fidelity prototype
concepts.definition: A low-fidelity prototype is a prototype of an interface made without technological intervention, programming, code, or a computer, using non-digital materials such as paper, cardboard, or wood, and to represent interaction it needs a series of interface sketches, often called a storyboard, rather than a single sketch.

defining_facts.text: A low-fidelity prototype is a prototype created without technological intervention, programming, code, or a computer, using non-digital materials such as paper, cardboard, or wood, and paper mockups of the look, feel, and functionality of an interface are a popular example.

To represent interaction, a low-fidelity prototype needs a series of interface sketches rather than a single sketch, a practice often called storyboarding; a single sketch gives a horizontal prototype, whereas a series of sketches can give a vertical prototype depicting interaction.

concepts.name: storyboard
concepts.definition: A storyboard is a low-fidelity prototype consisting of a series of interface sketches, each a keyframe, that captures the sequence of user actions and screen changes for a specific task from beginning to end.

defining_facts.text: To represent interaction, a low-fidelity prototype needs a series of interface sketches rather than a single sketch, a practice often called storyboarding; a single sketch gives a horizontal prototype, whereas a series of sketches can give a vertical prototype depicting interaction.

In a storyboard, each sketch is a keyframe, which is a snapshot of the interaction at a particular point in time; the keyframes visualize the interaction for a specific task and its corresponding scenes, and the storyboard captures the sequence of user actions and the screen appearances the user sees from the beginning of the task to its end.

A low-fidelity prototype for a cognitive walkthrough can be made as simple paper prototypes using the storyboarding approach, in which each prototype is a series of sketches depicting screen changes after each interaction, that is, a storyboard.

never_defined.name: graphical user interface
never_defined.definition: Graphical user interface (GUI) is a drag-and-drop interface that most standalone augmented reality authoring tools provide to allow users with basic personal computer skills to create applications without coding.

never_defined.name: interface
never_defined.definition: An interface is the way a system interfaces with users, its environment, and other systems, letting users provide input, see outcomes, and act on outcomes; on a computer screen it is the whole content seen there.

never_defined.name: system design
never_defined.definition: System design is the part of interactive system development in which user characteristics, usability requirements, and observed user activities are used to plan system features.

never_defined.name: end user
never_defined.definition: End user is involved in interactive system development from the requirement-gathering stage onward, usually distinct from the client, and usability requirements primarily come from the end user.

never_defined.name: usability testing
never_defined.definition: Usability testing is a systematic empirical study that involves users to estimate whether an interactive system is usable, distinct from code testing, which only shows that a system is executable.

never_defined.name: low-fidelity cardboard mockup
never_defined.definition: A Low-fidelity cardboard mockup is mainly suitable for throwaway prototypes because it is less costly and discarding it does not incur significant cost.

never_defined.name: paper sketch
never_defined.definition: A paper sketch is mainly suitable for throwaway prototypes because it is less costly and discarding it does not incur significant cost.

never_defined.name: module
never_defined.definition: A module is a part into which a system design divides a system for an incremental prototype, and each module is prototyped and tested separately before the modules are integrated into the overall system.

never_defined.name: robust evaluation technique
never_defined.definition: A robust evaluation technique is an evaluation technique that typically involves suitably skilled evaluators, resources, and an evaluation setup.

never_defined.name: evaluator
never_defined.definition: An evaluator is a skilled person who examines a prototype and reports usability issues or heuristic violations.

never_defined.name: evaluation setup
never_defined.definition: Evaluation setup is one of the things typically involved in a robust evaluation technique.

never_defined.name: design team
never_defined.definition: A Design team is a team that can serve as the evaluation team for quick or expert evaluation and that can combine evaluators' usability issue reports into a final list of usability issues.

never_defined.name: skilled designer
never_defined.definition: A skilled designer is a designer with knowledge and skill in the problem domain who may be part of an evaluation team for quick or expert evaluation.

never_defined.name: problem domain
never_defined.definition: Problem domain is the subject area in which skilled designers have knowledge and skill for quick or expert evaluation.

never_defined.name: domain expert
never_defined.definition: A domain expert is someone relied on for quick or expert evaluation instead of end users, because engaging them is less complicated, quicker, and cheaper than engaging a full evaluation team with end users.

never_defined.name: usability issue
never_defined.definition: Usability issue is a problem in the usability of an interface or prototype that evaluators identify during evaluations, and that users are likely to face while performing tasks.

never_defined.name: usability inspection
never_defined.definition: Usability inspection is a method in which usability problems are identified by inspecting a prototype.

never_defined.name: low-fidelity vertical prototype
never_defined.definition: A low-fidelity vertical prototype is a prototype that supports several tasks and is the minimum required for a cognitive walkthrough.

never_defined.name: high-fidelity prototype
never_defined.definition: A high-fidelity prototype is a prototype that is more welcome for a cognitive walkthrough but involves more time and cost.

never_defined.name: paper prototype
never_defined.definition: A paper prototype is a simple, low-fidelity prototype for a cognitive walkthrough, made as a storyboard: a series of sketches showing screen changes after each interaction.

never_defined.name: scenario
never_defined.definition: A Scenario is a description of a task created for evaluators in a cognitive walkthrough, whose described task is converted into the actions that must be performed in a prototype.

never_defined.name: usability question
never_defined.definition: A usability question is a question framed before a cognitive walkthrough to reflect usability issues; evaluators use it as a guideline to identify likely user problems and must answer it with a detailed report rather than a simple yes-or-no response.

never_defined.name: report
never_defined.definition: A report is a detailed answer that evaluators give for each usability question, rather than a simple yes or no answer, explaining where difficulty was felt in an interface or interaction and why, and it is collected, combined, and analyzed to identify broader usability issues.

never_defined.name: evaluation session
never_defined.definition: An evaluation session is a session at the end of which evaluators' reports are collected, combined, and analyzed to identify broader usability issues.

never_defined.name: checklist
never_defined.definition: A checklist is a list of heuristics used in heuristic evaluation to assess a prototype or interface by checking whether each heuristic is followed or violated. Checklists can be detailed and system-specific, or focused on broader usability principles, and broader checklists contain fewer heuristics.

never_defined.name: heuristic
never_defined.definition: A heuristic is a checklist item that is used in heuristic evaluation to assess a prototype and determine whether the heuristic is followed or violated.

never_defined.name: task scenario
never_defined.definition: A task scenario is something not used in heuristic evaluation, in which evaluators assess a presented prototype by ticking items on a checklist of heuristics to perform a comprehensive evaluation of the whole system rather than a task-specific evaluation.

never_defined.name: task performance
never_defined.definition: Task performance is part of a task-specific evaluation, whereas heuristic evaluation assesses a whole system without a task scenario or task performance.

never_defined.name: system-specific checklist
never_defined.definition: A system-specific checklist is a detailed checklist for evaluating an interface.

never_defined.name: usability principle
never_defined.definition: A usability principle is one of the broader principles that checklists focus on when evaluating interfaces.

never_defined.name: broader checklist
never_defined.definition: A broader checklist is a checklist for evaluating interfaces that focuses on broader usability principles, contains fewer heuristics, and is not specific to any particular interface.

never_defined.name: flexibility and efficiency of use
never_defined.definition: Flexibility and efficiency of use is one of Nielsen's 10 heuristics.

introduced.name: match between system and the real world
help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors
